fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I started my PhD, this was around the time deep RL was really taking off. You had the DQN work on Atari, and a couple years later AlphaGo, and it was genuinely exciting. But if you actually looked at what made those systems work, there were a few assumptions baked in that just don't hold once you step outside of games.

The first one was sample efficiency. These agents were learning from tens of millions of frames. You can do that in a simulator where the environment is free and you can reset it. You can't do that if the environment is a real user, or a web browser hitting a real website, or a robot that breaks when it falls over. So the question of where the agent gets its knowledge from, if not from trial and error, was sort of the elephant in the room.

The second thing, and this is the one I ended up spending a lot of time on, was that the agent starts from nothing. It has no prior about the world. A classical RL agent playing a text adventure game doesn't know that a key opens a door or that fire is dangerous. It has to discover that by dying a thousand times. Whereas a human sitting down to play that game brings all this background knowledge, and a lot of that knowledge is expressed in language. So I was interested in language as a way to inject priors, to transfer across tasks, to let you say what you want instead of hand-designing a reward function. Reward specification was the other big gap. In Atari the score is just given to you. In almost any real application, the hard part is actually saying what good behavior looks like, and people naturally want to do that in words, not in a scalar.

And then the last piece was generalization. RL agents were being trained and tested on the same environment, basically. Change the level layout, change the object names, and it falls apart. If you want to deploy something, it has to handle situations it hasn't seen. Again, language seemed like the right abstraction, because a description of a task or a manual for an environment is a compact thing that generalizes in ways pixels don't.

So the thesis I was pushing was, roughly, that you can't just scale up the trial-and-error part. You need something that gives the agent knowledge for free, and language is the most natural vehicle for that. In hindsight that's basically what pretraining turned out to be. The GPT work was in some sense the answer to the first question, where does the prior come from, and then a lot of what we've done since has been about connecting that prior back to the decision-making side.

opus-5.5.text:
Classical reinforcement learning has a beautiful formulation. You have an agent, an environment, actions, and a reward, and in principle you can learn anything from that loop. When I started my PhD at MIT, though, what struck me was how far that framework was from what you'd need to deploy something in the real world.

The biggest gap was prior knowledge. Classical RL agents learn everything from scratch. They start knowing nothing about the world and figure it out through millions of interactions. That works in Atari or Go, where you can simulate as many episodes as you want. In a practical setting, whether you're interacting with people, operating software, or controlling something physical, you can't afford millions of trial-and-error attempts. Humans don't learn that way either. When you pick up a new video game or a new tool, you bring a huge amount of background knowledge about how the world works, what objects do, and what instructions mean.

That led to my interest in language. Much of that knowledge is encoded in language: manuals, instructions, descriptions of the world. One of the earliest things I worked on was text-based games, where the state of the world and the actions are all described in natural language. Very quickly you see that the agent's problem isn't just maximizing reward. It has to understand what the text means. If the game says "you're in a dark room and there's a locked door to the north," a human knows to look for a key or a light. A classical RL agent has to stumble on that through random exploration.

So the missing piece, as I saw it, was a way to inject semantic understanding and world knowledge into the agent, so it isn't learning tabula rasa. A related problem was generalization. Agents trained in one environment tended to overfit badly and couldn't transfer to a slightly different setting. Language seemed like a natural bridge, because it's compositional and abstract. If you understand "key opens door" in one game, that should carry over to another.

Reward specification was also hard. In practical applications you rarely have a clean scalar reward handed to you. Someone has to design it, and it's often sparse or misaligned with what you actually want. Being able to describe goals or give feedback in language felt like a much more natural interface than hand-engineering reward functions.

That line of thinking, that you need a strong prior learned from huge amounts of text, eventually fed into the motivation for generative pre-training. If you could get a model to absorb the knowledge in language first, then RL or fine-tuning on top of it becomes much more tractable. In hindsight that's roughly how things played out with today's systems: a pre-trained language model as the foundation, with reinforcement learning layered on top.

fable-5.text:
When I started working with RL back in grad school, the thing that struck me immediately was how everything started from scratch. The classic setup is tabula rasa — you drop an agent into an environment, it knows nothing, and it has to learn purely from trial and error, from this very sparse reward signal. And that works if you can afford millions of interactions, like in Atari or Go, where you have a perfect simulator and failure is free. But almost no practical application looks like that. You can't have a robot break ten thousand dishes, and you can't have a software agent crash your production system a million times while it figures things out.

So sample efficiency was the obvious problem, but I came to think of it as a symptom of something deeper, which is that these agents had no prior knowledge about the world. Humans don't learn this way. If I give you a new video game, you don't flail randomly — you read the instructions, you know that keys open doors and spikes are bad, you bring in this huge amount of background knowledge, a lot of it transmitted through language. That's actually what drew me to working on text-based games and language grounding: language is this incredibly compact way to inject priors into an agent and get generalization across environments, instead of relearning everything every time the environment shifts slightly.

And the other piece that's underrated is reward specification. In the benchmarks, the reward is handed to you — score goes up, you win the game. In the real world, defining what you actually want is often the hardest part of the problem, and classical RL just assumed that away. So you had this field with beautiful mathematical foundations, but the assumptions — unlimited interaction, no prior knowledge, a clean reward function — were almost exactly the opposite of what practical applications demand. A lot of my work since, and honestly a lot of what made language models so interesting to me, has been about attacking that gap: getting the knowledge in first, and then letting the agent learn on top of it.

opus-5.text:
Two things, really, and they're related.

The first is that classical RL is almost aggressively tabula rasa. You drop an agent into an environment and it has to rediscover everything from scratch — that fire is bad, that keys open doors, that if you've tried a strategy ten times and it hasn't worked it probably won't work the eleventh. Humans don't do that. We walk into a new situation carrying an enormous amount of prior knowledge about how the world tends to behave, and most of that knowledge we acquired through language — we read it, someone told us, we picked it up secondhand. So the sample complexity numbers you see in the Atari papers aren't really a statement about how hard those games are. They're a statement about how expensive it is to learn without priors.

The second thing is generalization. The classic setup trains and tests in the same MDP. You tune a policy on one environment and it's genuinely good at that environment, and then you perturb it slightly — change the layout, rename the objects, swap the dynamics a little — and performance falls off a cliff. For anything you'd actually want to deploy, that's disqualifying, because the real world is a distribution of tasks, not one task.

What drew me to language was that it seemed like a handle on both problems at once. Text is a compressed description of structure in the world, and it's compositional, so a representation grounded in language has some chance of transferring to a situation you haven't seen. That's a very different bet than just making the function approximator bigger or the exploration bonus cleverer — those help, but they don't get you out of the tabula rasa trap.

sonnet-5.5.text:
When I was working on RL back then, the thing that bothered me was that these agents started from nothing. You'd put an agent in an Atari game or a simulated environment, and it would spend millions of interactions figuring out things a person already knows, like what a key does or that you shouldn't walk into lava. Humans never learn that way. We bring a huge amount of prior knowledge to a new task, and a lot of it comes through language: someone tells us what to do, we read a manual, we pick up instructions.

So for me there were two gaps. The first was sample efficiency and transfer. Classical RL treated every environment as a blank slate, so you couldn't take what you learned in one game and carry it to another. The second was that all the task information had to be squeezed through a reward function. Writing a good reward is hard, and for most real-world problems the reward is sparse or badly specified. A lot of what we want an agent to do is easy to say in words and awkward to encode as a number.

That's what got me interested in text-based games. They were a clean testbed where the state, the actions, and the instructions are all language, so you could ask whether an agent can use language to ground what it's doing and generalize better. But it also made clear that if you want an agent to have broad prior knowledge, you need to get it from somewhere other than the environment's reward signal. The obvious place is the huge amount of text already out there.

That's the line of thought that connects to the GPT work. If you pretrain a model on a lot of unlabeled text, you get a general prior about the world and about language, and then you can adapt it to specific tasks with far less supervision. In some sense it was the missing ingredient for RL, a way to start from something instead of from scratch. Of course, it took a while for us to figure out how to bring those two threads back together properly, but that was the original frustration.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap was that classical RL starts from almost nothing. An agent learns by trial and error from a scalar reward, and that works in a tidy simulator with a clear score and cheap interaction. Most practical problems have none of those properties. Rewards are sparse or hard to write down, every experiment costs real time or money, and the agent has no common-sense knowledge about the world it's acting in.

What struck me was how much of that prior knowledge already exists in language. A person can read a short description of a task and immediately know what success looks like and which actions are plausible. Classical agents had no way to take advantage of that, so they spent most of their training budget rediscovering things any human would take for granted.

That's why I got interested in using language as a bridge: as a way to specify goals, supply priors, and let an agent generalize to tasks it hasn't seen. I wouldn't say language solves the problem. Grounding it in actual behavior is still hard, and I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet. But the mismatch between what RL assumed and what practitioners actually had was a big part of what pushed me in that direction.

astra-6.text:
The big missing piece, to me, was a way to use prior knowledge. In the standard reinforcement learning setup, you give an agent a reward signal, and it learns through trial and error. But if it has to learn everything from scratch, that can require an enormous amount of interaction, which is expensive in real applications.

Humans don’t learn that way. We bring an understanding of the world, and we can read instructions or have someone explain what to do. Language is a really powerful way to communicate that knowledge. So the question is: can we give an agent that same advantage, so it can learn faster and apply what it knows to new situations?

sol-6.1.text:
The big thing was prior knowledge. In the classical reinforcement learning setup, you put an agent in an environment, give it a reward signal, and it has to figure everything out through trial and error. That’s a useful abstraction, but in practical applications you often can’t afford that much exploration. A robot can’t break thousands of objects before it learns how to handle them.

Humans don’t learn that way exclusively. We can read instructions, ask someone for help, or take something we learned in another setting and apply it to a new problem. Language is a really natural way to communicate that knowledge.

So the question for me was: can we build agents that use language to guide their learning and decisions? They should still learn from experience, but they shouldn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch.
